questions.q: If log-returns ln(Sₜ/Sₜ₋₁) are modeled as i.i.d. normal, what distribution does the price Sₜ itself follow?
questions.explain: A variable whose logarithm is normally distributed is, by definition, lognormally distributed. This is why asset prices (which must stay positive) are modeled as lognormal when log-returns are modeled as normal.

questions.q: A Student's t-distribution with ν = 4 degrees of freedom is fit to return data instead of a normal distribution. What is the main practical benefit?
options: It forces the mean to be exactly zero
It has heavier tails than the normal, better matching the excess kurtosis seen in real returns
It eliminates the need to estimate variance
questions.explain: The Student's t-distribution has heavier tails than the normal for finite degrees of freedom, converging to the normal only as ν → ∞. Lower ν means fatter tails, which better captures the excess kurtosis typical of financial returns.

questions.q: For a Poisson-distributed count of defaults with rate λ = 3 per year, what are the mean and variance of the count?
questions.explain: For a Poisson distribution, E[N] = Var(N) = λ. With λ = 3, both the mean and variance equal 3.

questions.q: What does the "memoryless" property of the exponential distribution state?
options: The distribution has no defined mean
P(X > s + t | X > s) = P(X > t) — time already elapsed gives no information about remaining waiting time
Every observation must be independent of the sample mean
questions.explain: Memorylessness means the conditional probability of waiting at least t more time, given you've already waited s, is the same as the unconditional probability of waiting at least t — the exponential distribution 'forgets' how long you've already waited.

questions.q: A Pareto distribution has tail index α = 1.5. What does this imply about its variance?
options: The variance is finite and equals 1.5
The variance is infinite, since finite variance requires α > 2
The variance cannot be determined from α alone
questions.explain: A Pareto distribution has finite variance only when α > 2. With α = 1.5 ≤ 2, the variance is infinite — exactly the regime where the classical Central Limit Theorem no longer applies to sums of such variables.
